catalog_quote: There are three indications that the original stress system in Umpithamu must have been one that was left-aligned, with a leftmost stress rule. The first indication is local, relating to Umpithamu’s closest relatives. Most other Middle Paman languages for which we have a reliable description of word stress have a system of this kind: this is the case, for instance, in Wik Mungkan (Kilham 1974), Kugu Nganhcara (Smith & Johnson 2000), Wik Ngathan (Sutton 1978) and possibly also Umpila (Thompson 1988).5 [fn. 5: There are some complications in Umpila relating to syllable weight (due to the occurrence of vowel length beyond the first syllable).] ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand: Kugu Nganhcara (the patrilect cluster that includes Kugu Mu'inh) is reported, on the authority of Smith & Johnson 2000, to have a left-aligned system with primary stress assigned by a leftmost rule, i.e. on the word-initial syllable. The only first-hand prosodic remark reachable (Smith 1986: 517, on the sister patrilect Kugu Muminh, seen via IA search snippets) says the language 'is a syllable-timed language, though initial syllables are about 20% longer than comparable non-initial syllables', contrasting it with Wik Munkan where 'initial syllables are rhythmically strong (i.e. stressed)' -- so initial prominence in Nganhcara is weak/durational rather than a strong dynamic stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing specific to Kugu Nganhcara; Verstraete notes only the general Pama-Nyungan reports of alternating secondary stress (and the 'stress ghosting' caveat).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kugu Nganhcara. Smith & Johnson 1986 note vowel length is generally restricted to initial syllables (consistent with initial prominence); Smith 1986 and Evans 1995 characterise the language as syllable-timed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level typological summary by a third party; the primary statement (Smith & Johnson 2000, HAL vol. 5) was not seen, so the exact formulation, domain (root vs word, treatment of enclitics, compounds) and any caveat about weak stress remain unverified.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements found refer to Kugu Nganhcara as a whole (Glottolog cover languoid wikn1246 'Wikngenchera'; WALS knc), the cluster of six or seven mutually intelligible patrilects of which Kuku-Mu'inh (kuku1282, xmp) is one; Smith & Johnson 1986 say the patrilects 'differ in only minor aspects of their morphology and phonology' (Mu'inh-specific: alveolars realised as retroflexes). The one first-hand prosodic remark (Smith 1986) is specifically about the sister patrilect Kugu Muminh (kuku1283, xmh) as spoken at Edward River. No source seen describes Mu'inh prosody separately.

sources.citation: Sutton, Peter & Ken Hale. 2021. Linguistic Organisation and Native Title: The Wik Case, Australia. Canberra: ANU Press (open access).
sources.note: Hale's ch. 7 has a Kugu Nganhcara pronominal/enclitic section but no statement on KN word stress; stress remarks concern Wik-Me'nh/Mungkan/Ngathan (free pronouns stressed, enclitics atonic; Sutton's fn.: first-syllable vowel carries primary word stress in Wik-Ngathan/Ngatharr orthography note).

sources.citation: Smith, Ian & Steve Johnson. 1986. Sociolinguistic patterns in an unstratified society: the patrilects of Kugu Nganhcara. Journal of the Atlantic Provinces Linguistic Association 8: 29-43.
sources.note: Silent on stress. Sec. 3.1 gives the inventory; long/short vowel contrast 'generally restricted to initial syllables'; Mu'inh and Iyanh realise alveolar obstruents as retroflexes; patrilects 'differ in only minor aspects of their morphology and phonology'.
38 datapoints all coded from Smith & Johnson 2000; no stress features (14A-17A absent), so not in StressTyp/WALS stress chapters.
